strings.Here’s the screen to check who’s buying: Here’s the screen to check who’s buying your computers and where they live. At the top, you see the user groups and below that the economy level of their countries. Remember, different user groups want different things. Casuals are the baseline, they just want solid all-around computers. Gamers care about less heat and better CPU, Memory, and Graphics, especially their performance and capacity. Workers focus on low noise and value features and ease-of-use in Displays and Operating Systems. Cheapskaters, or bargain hunters, will usually pick the cheapest options.  User group sizes change with the country’s economy. Casuals are always the biggest group, at least 45 percent. Gamers make up only 18 percent in poor countries but jump to 42 percent in rich ones. Cheapskaters stay a small minority, about 12 percent in poor countries but almost zero in wealthy ones. Keep this in mind when picking your next market.

strings.Home Computers were the first wave. Simp: Home Computers were the first wave. Simple machines for families, mostly used for games, schoolwork, and typing. They felt a lot like early consoles because you couldn’t upgrade them much, and they mostly ran whatever came built-in or on cartridges, cassettes, or floppy disks later. People didn’t take them too seriously, which is why...  Personal Computers became the next big term. It was a rebranding to make computers sound more serious and business-friendly. Companies didn’t want “toys,” so calling them “personal” made them easier to sell for office use. They were supposed to be modular, meaning you could swap out parts, but early on, compatibility was a mess - so it was more of a marketing promise than reality.  Portable Computers were meant to be used on the go, but early models were still pretty bulky. Think of a big briefcase or coffer. You could technically carry them, but you wouldn't want to walk far with one.  Handheld Computers finally made computers pocket-sized. Think of PDAs and eventually smartphones. They gave you real computing power in your hands - used on the couch, in bed, on the train, or yes, even on the toilet.  All of today’s devices still fit into these four categories. Consoles? Just Home Computers for gaming. Smartphones? Just modern Handhelds. These labels are mostly marketing. In the end, they’re all just computers.

strings.In Computer Tycoon you have 4 main resou: In Computer Tycoon you have 4 main resources: money and 3 different kinds of points. The points are generated at your Sites by your Departments. RP is for Research Points, LP is for Logistic Points and PP is for Production Points. The more RPs you have, the faster you can get new technologies, the more LPs you have the more Markets you can sell in, and the more PPs you have the more Computers you can produce per day.
strings.In Computer Tycoon, I wanted to add a me:
In Computer Tycoon, I wanted to add a mechanic that lets you spend your hard-earned millions. What do you get for your money? Pictures. That’s it.

Why? Most business games let you make tons of money, then make even more with that money. Sounds familiar, right? After a while, having that much cash is pointless - there’s nothing left to do with it. If that’s enough for you, just ignore this feature. Your call.

But if you want more, now you can reward yourself with things. A house, a car, some fancy objects... they can be yours! Enjoy it. Just remember, you’re spending your business’s money. You can’t get it back or sell these items. This makes the game a bit more interesting and pushes you to be a more focused, dependable entrepreneur. Plus, it’s another reason to chase those billions.

Have fun, my friend!
Andris aka Progorion - the solo developer of Computer Tycoon

strings.On the Pricing Screen you can see a fiel: On the Pricing Screen you can see a field called "Base Price". Whatever you set here will be discounted regionally, so it should be high. I usually set it to $8000 for Home Computers. You also have a matrix about the discounts per Economy Status. People living in a Poor Market have a lower budget to buy a Computer than others living in Rich Markets. I usually leave the discounts on the default 75,65,50,40,0 percent accordingly. That is my preference, but you should find yours.
strings.On the Product’s Marketing page, you set: On the Product’s Marketing page, you set your Campaign’s Preference, Channel Focus, and Main Target Group. Preference sliders depend on your Product’s Design and the Main Target Group. Channel Focus depends on the Campaign’s size and the Main Target Group. As long as you have a Computer on the market, you must pay for its marketing. If sales are low, it’s better to archive the product and lower your factory budget to save money. You can have up to 3 computers from the same Design (like Home Computer) on the market at once, but this adds Extra Overhead Cost. Building Marketing Departments at your Sites reduces campaign costs. Each computer has one campaign. Every time you release a new computer, after a month you get a new hint for your sliders on this screen. Hints change as you adjust settings, so keep an eye on them.
strings.On the Reviews screen, you see opinions: On the Reviews screen, you see opinions from five important magazines about your computer. CompDEALS is serious about price, so you could call it the magazine of the Cheapskates. Computer World reflects Casual users, while Popular Electronics represents the geeks - your potential fans. The Economist is for CEOs in other industries, so if they like your product, workers might start paying attention. And Gamer’s Rig? That one speaks for itself.
strings.On the left side of the \"Hardware Desig: On the left side of the "Hardware Designer" window you can see a preview of your Hardware and under it there is a list of available technologies. There are mandatory technologies and optional ones. Don't worry if you miss a mandatory one, the game will warn you about it! Add the technologies to your Storage by clicking on them and see how the stats of your Storage are changing.
strings.On the other panel, you can select a dep: On the other panel, you can select a department such as the “Factory Department”. Here you can see its actual stats and future level stats. Every upgrade has an upfront cost and an upkeep cost as well. On this panel you can see the base prices, while later on the budget window you can see the actual (bonus affected) costs, too. Also, some departments have special requirements such as other department levels. Push the Build button to start the construction!
strings.On the tech Tree, you can see how techno: On the tech Tree, you can see how technology will evolve in the future and you can plan things out, while on the tech queue you see only the next available pieces of technology. If you double click on a technology on the Tree, then it will add the given technology and all its requirements to the Queue. The amount of technology might seem like a lot, but you can just think about what sections of your computer you'd like to improve (motherboard, cpu, power supply, etc.), or you can just think about the functionality group you'd like to invest money in (data projection, computing, manufacturing, etc.) and you can focus on those. As soon as a company invents something, the newly invented technology will automatically have a lower research price, so you should readjust your research queue time after time. Also, a good goal is to unlock the PC design or the portable design, because the first company pushing out a new type of computer design will have a big advantage in the market, so you can aim for that, too!
strings.On this level of semiconductor process t: On this level of semiconductor process technology many more transistors can be placed on a wafer. The lower the number, the more we can put on the chip; that results in faster chips!
strings.On this screen you can track your sales: On this screen you can track your sales graph and some financial data for your computer. Remember, after a computer has been on the market for a month, you’ll get a new hint on your Product Marketing screen.
strings.On this screen you could just select an: On this screen you could just select an already existing hardware part and add it to your computer (if you made one earlier), or you can click on the "New" button to make a new one.
strings.On this screen, you can compare your com: On this screen, you can compare your computer with other models and get more insight into what’s driving your sales.
strings.On this screen, you can give or receive: On this screen, you can give or receive gifts. Gifts help improve your relationship with other players. Use them to avoid rivals or even make friends. Want a better chance of your opponent signing a research contract? Try giving some gifts.
strings.On this screen, you can sue an opponent: On this screen, you can sue an opponent who committed a crime against you. Choose the cause of action and your strategy, and see the rewards if you win. If you lose, you lose only the costs you paid - and your opponent gets 50% of the fan boost you would have earned.
strings.On this screen, you can trade technology: On this screen, you can trade technology and blueprints with your opponents. Once you get a technology or blueprint from someone, you can’t trade it to others, and they can’t trade what they got from you — you only get a license to use it. A blueprint is a hardware design players can build into their computers. But remember, you can’t take individual tech from a blueprint and mix it into other parts. You can only produce the exact hardware described in that blueprint.
strings.On this screen, you or your opponent can: On this screen, you or your opponent can make demands. Demands let you get stuff for free, but they hurt your relationship. Once one demand is accepted by either side, neither of you can make another demand or declare rivalry for 15 years. So, who will make the first move? And who needs that neutral relationship more?

strings.Red elements are mandatory for your comp: Red elements are mandatory for your computer.  Once all required parts are in place, hit “Create Prototype” to start polishing. This takes 30 days, and each Design Type reacts differently. You can wait it out or skip straight to production with the “Market” button, which turns your design into a product you can advertise and sell.  Early in the game, technology limits make it hard to create truly different models. That means selling multiple at the same time can backfire because they will cannibalize each other's sales.  User groups look at main properties like Features or Performance. For example, workers prefer ease of use. They also pay attention to specific parts separately. Gamers, for instance, care more about GPUs. It matters where your performance boost comes from, whether it is the GPU or removable media. The biggest group, casual users, are the exception because they just care about the main properties.

strings.Registered (also called buffered) memory: Registered (also called buffered) memory modules have a register between the DRAM modules and the system's memory controller. They place less electrical load on the memory controller and allow single systems to remain stable with more memory modules than they would have otherwise. More expensive, but more robust! Gives 1.5x performance for the given memory.

strings.This screen shows who’s buying your comp: This screen shows who’s buying your computers and where they live. On top, you see the user groups, below that the economy level of their countries. Different groups want different things. Casuals are the base—they care mostly about main features. Gamers want computers that run cooler with better CPU, Memory, and Graphics, focusing on performance and capacity. Workers are sensitive to noise and look for features and ease-of-use in Displays and Operating Systems. Cheapskaters just go for the cheapest options. The size of these groups depends on the country’s economy. Casuals always make up at least 45%. Gamers are just 18% in poor countries but jump to 42% in rich ones. Cheapskaters stay a small minority, about 12% in poor countries but only 0.01% in rich ones. Keep this in mind when picking your next market.
strings.This screen tells you if your market gen: This screen tells you if your market generates enough money to pay for its own costs, and how much profit it makes on top of that. The Average Local Market Profit tells you if it can pay for only its own costs (how much did cost the production of the sold computers and how much product marketing was needed here), while the global market profit field tells you if the market can also pay for its share of the other company costs as well. When your Avg. Global Company Profit per 1m people is negative, it doesn't mean automatically that you shouldn't sell in the country, but tells you that in relation to the population of this market other markets are definitely more profitable. But when your Avg. Local Market Profit per 1m people is negative, then you make a loss for sure. For more details, hover over the labels.
